You write your domain in Rust and mark it with a handful of attributes. Keel generates idiomatic Swift, Kotlin and TypeScript from the schema those attributes produce, so the UI stays SwiftUI, Compose and React. Each platform keeps a local mirror of your state, so reads never cross the language boundary. A write crosses once per transaction, and the core answers with one compact binary change-set that patches every mirror. Where these pages come from. Everything here is digested from the repository: the README, the specification in docs/SPEC.md, the onboarding guide, the benchmark results and the playground app. When a page and the spec disagree, the spec wins; the repository is the record.

State in Keel lives in the Rust core as signals inside stores. Platforms hold a local mirror, reads never cross the boundary, and a write crosses once per transaction.

Everything a platform can see is one of eight kinds of thing, each declared with an attribute. They cross the boundary in one of two ways: by value (copied) or by handle (a reference to something that stays in the core). Concept Declared with Crosses Record #[keel::api] on a struct by value Enum #[keel::api] on an enum, unit or data variants by value Error #[keel::error] on an enum; adds Display and std::error::Error by value Object #[keel::api] on an impl block; methods are sync or async by handle Store an object whose struct has #[keel::store]; its signals are mirrored by handle Port #[keel::port] on a trait; implemented by the platform or by a Rust fake the core calls out to it Query, mutation #[keel::query], #[keel::mutation] on an async fn managed by the query client Function #[keel::api] on a free fn like a method with no receiver The rest of this page is about stores, because that is where reactive state lives.

A store is a struct of signals with an impl block that says what the platforms can call. The to-do list from the playground is a complete example: core/src/todos.rs #[keel::store(restore = "Self::assemble")] pub struct Todos { next: AtomicU64, // private state: not a signal #[keel(key = "id")] todos: Signal<Vec<Todo>>, // signal 0 filter: Signal<Filter>, // signal 1 visible: Computed<Vec<Todo>>, // signal 2, derived remaining: Computed<u32>, // signal 3, derived } #[keel::api(store)] impl Todos { pub fn new(ctx: Ctx) -> Self { /* … */ } pub async fn add(&self, title: String) -> Result<Todo, TodoError> { /* … */ } pub fn toggle(&self, id: Uuid) { /* … */ } pub fn set_filter(&self, filter: Filter) { self.filter.set(filter); } } A few rules worth knowing up front: Signals are the fields of type Signal<T> and Computed<T>, numbered in declaration order (0, 1, 2, …). Other fields are private state: a Ctx, a counter, configuration. A store needs a constructor, a pub fn returning Self or Result<Self, E>. Generated code calls it to create the object in the core and gets back a handle. Receivers are &self. Objects are shared, so mutation goes through signals or a lock. &mut self is rejected …

A Signal<T> holds a value. You read it with get() (a clone) or with(|v| …) (a borrow), and write it with set(value) or update(|v| …). rust self.filter.set(Filter::Done); // replace self.todos.update(|list| list.retain(|t| !t.done)); // edit in place let open = self.todos.with(|list| list.iter().filter(|t| !t.done).count()); A write outside a transaction is an implicit single-write transaction, so the change is committed and delivered at once. Inside update, the closure holds the value's write lock: it must not read or write the same signal, or read a computed derived from it. A violation panics with a clear message instead of deadlocking.

A Computed<T> is a value derived from signals. You name its inputs and give it a function of them: rust let visible = Computed::new((&todos, &filter), |(todos, filter)| { todos.iter().filter(|t| filter.matches(t)).cloned().collect() }); let remaining = Computed::new(&todos, |todos| todos.iter().filter(|t| !t.done).count() as u32); Inputs are &Signal<A> or &Computed<A>, or a tuple of up to six of them, and the closure receives references. A computed is recomputed in the core, in dependency order, and pushed in the same change-set as the write that caused it. The UI never derives anything itself, so it cannot disagree with the core about, say, how many items are left. Because a store with computeds cannot be rebuilt from its plain signals automatically, you name a function that assembles it: #[keel::store(restore = "Self::assemble")]. The macro tells you when you forget (E0013).

When several signals change together, group the writes. Everything inside ctx.txn commits as one transaction, so observers see one consistent change-set and never a half-applied state. The playground's counter changes two signals and derives a third: core/src/counter.rs pub fn add(&self, amount: i32) { self.ctx.txn(|| { self.count.update(|c| *c = c.saturating_add(amount)); self.changes.update(|n| *n = n.saturating_add(1)); }); // one change-set carries count, changes and parity } Transactions nest: an inner txn joins the outer one. A change-set is never split, and change-sets are delivered in commit order; for one store they reach the platform one at a time with strictly increasing transaction ids.

A platform does not receive everything. It observes signals, and only observed signals that changed are sent. Two details follow from that: Observing sends the current value right away, before the call returns in-process, so a store's initial state arrives as an ordinary change-set. A signal written while unobserved is remembered as pending and sent when someone starts observing it. Only what changed is sent. Writing filter in the to-do store ships filter and the recomputed visible, and nothing else, because todos did not change. A signal marked #[keel(no_coalesce)] is delivered on every commit instead of being folded into the latest value. A change-set is a compact binary structure, described on the architecture page. For side effects that belong in the core, Effect::new(deps, f) runs f after each commit that dirtied one of its dependencies, and is cancelled when dropped.

A Signal<Vec<T>> marked #[keel(key = "field")] is a keyed list. The key is the identity of a row, and the core sends changes to it as a patch of positional operations instead of the whole list. Operation Meaning Insert { index, item } put the item at index Remove { index } take the row at index out Update { index, item } replace the row at index Move { from, to } take the row at from, then place it so it ends at to Clear empty the list The platform applies the operations in order to its own copy of the list. If a patch ever disagrees with that copy (an index out of bounds), the platform treats the signal as out of sync and observes it again, which resends the full value.

h: Why a list write costs the change, not the list
x: How the core produces the patch decides the cost. There are two ways. Recorded operations are the fast path. Signal<Vec<T>> has push, insert, remove, update_at, move_item and clear. Each one mutates the list and appends the operation it performed to a log; at commit, that log is the patch. No key is hashed and no item is compared, so the cost is the change, not the length of the list. examples/playground/core/src/biglist.rs /// Inserts a new row so that it ends at `index`. One keyed `Insert`. pub fn insert_at(&self, index: u32, label: String) -> Result<u32, ListError> { // …check the index… let id = self.next_id.fetch_add(1, Ordering::Relaxed); self.items.insert(index as usize, Item { id, label, version: 0 }); Ok(id) } Raw writes (set, update, replace) are the fallback. They are always correct, but the core cannot know what you did, so at commit it diffs the new list against what the platform has: hash every key, compare the surviving rows. That is O(list). It also falls back to sending the whole value when the two lists share no key, a key occurs twice, or more than half of the old rows were removed. The difference is measured. Each platform runtime holds a mirror: store handle, then signal id, then the decoded value. Generated code exposes the mirror in the platform's own idiom (an @Observable property, a StateFlow, a Signal with useSignal), so reading is a local memory read that never calls into the core. Every change-set is applied on the main thread, in one hop per transaction: Swift on the MainActor, Kotlin on Dispatchers.Main.immediate, and TypeScript in a queued flush on the page's main thread. A store is an object with a lifetime: release it explicitly with close() (Swift and Kotlin use deinit and a Cleaner as backstops, TypeScript a FinalizationRegistry), and KeelCore.stats() shows live handle counts.

The core can snapshot every store's plain signals (computeds are left out and recomputed) and restore them, which is how a web page recovers after a crash and how tests rebuild state. Restore keeps the same handles valid, so the platform's references keep working, and it cancels calls that were running on the stores it replaced. This is why the restore function above rebuilds computeds from signals, and why the to-do store continues its id counter above the largest id in the snapshot.

The core reads no clock and no random source and starts no thread of its own. Time comes from the Clock port, delays from ctx.sleep (which goes through the Timer port), randomness from Rng, the network from Http. That is rule R12, and it is why every scenario can be driven with deterministic fakes in Rust and with in-memory adapters on each platform. The to-do store's ids come from a counter for the same reason. See Ports & adapters.
Data fetching, caching and offline behaviour are not something each platform reimplements. They live in the core, next to the state they feed, and every platform observes the same cache.

h: Why the data layer is in the core
x: Fetching, caching, retrying, optimistic updates and offline queues are logic, and logic is what Keel writes once. The core never opens a socket: every request goes through the Http port, which is URLSession, OkHttp or fetch in an app and a scripted fake in a test. The query client keeps one cache that all platforms observe, so the to-do list on the iPhone and the one in a Chrome tab agree about what is fresh.

A query is an async fn whose first parameter is the Ctx, marked with #[keel::query]. This is the playground's remote to-do list, a GET that is cached per list: core/src/remote.rs /// The items of the server's list `list`: `GET {base}/lists/{list}/todos`. #[keel::query(key = "remote-todos:{list}", stale = "30s", persist, retry = 1)] pub async fn remote_todos(ctx: &Ctx, list: String) -> Result<Vec<RemoteTodo>, RemoteError> { let url = endpoint(ctx, &format!("/lists/{list}/todos"))?; parse(&send(ctx, HttpRequest::get(url)).await?) } Argument Meaning key = "…" the cache key; {param} placeholders name parameters, so two lists are two independent entries stale = "30s" how long a successful result stays fresh persist write the entry to the Kv port so it survives a restart retry = 3 how many times to retry a failed fetch idempotent (mutations) the request is safe to repeat, which makes it eligible for the offline queue The signature is checked when you compile: it must be async, take ctx: &Ctx first, and return Result<T, E>. A query whose success value is () or an Option is rejected, because a query caches a value and effects belong in a mutation (E0040 to E0042).

Platforms observe a query through a generated query handle, which is an ordinary store. For remote_todos it is RemoteTodosQueryHandle, and it has five signals: Signal Holds data the latest successful result, or nothing yet status idle, fetching, success or error error the error of the latest failed fetch, cleared by the next success fetching whether a request is in flight, also true while refetching stale data updatedAt when data last changed Constructing the handle registers an observer and starts a fetch if the entry is missing or stale. Releasing it removes the observer; when the last observer goes, the in-flight fetch is cancelled and the entry is kept for five minutes before it is garbage collected. The handle also has refetch() (fetch now, even if fresh) and invalidate() (mark stale; it refetches while observed). tsx const inbox = await RemoteTodosQueryHandle.create("inbox"); // observe const items = useSignal(inbox.data); // in a component const busy = useSignal(inbox.fetching);

An observed entry refetches when it is stale and something happens: an observer is added while it is stale, the app becomes Active again (the Lifecycle port), connectivity returns (the Connectivity port), its optional interval elapses, or it is invalidated, by key prefix. One fetch per key at a time. If five screens observe the same list, they share one in-flight request.

A failed fetch is retried retry times (three by default) with exponential backoff, min(1000 × 2ⁿ, 30000) milliseconds, with plus or minus 20% jitter. The jitter comes from the Rng port and the delay from the Timer port, so a test with fakes sees exactly the schedule it scripts.

A mutation is an async fn marked #[keel::mutation]. It shares its cache key with the query it affects. Call it through the context: rust ctx.mutate::<PostRemoteTodoMutation>((list, title)) .optimistic(move |cache| { cache.update::<RemoteTodosQuery>((cached,), |items| items.push(placeholder)); }) .invalidates(/* keys to mark stale */) .await optimistic runs inside a transaction with typed access to cache entries (get, set, update), so the UI shows the new item at once. On success the invalidates keys are marked stale and refetched if observed, which replaces the placeholder with the server's item. The playground wraps this in create_remote_todo and set_remote_done, which are what its three UIs call.

If the mutation fails, the optimistic write is undone, but only the writes that mutation made. Every cache entry carries a write stamp that changes with each write: an optimistic write, a set, or a fetch result. When a mutation fails, each entry it wrote is restored to what it was before, unless something else has written that entry since. An entry that was written since keeps that write. That rule is what makes concurrent mutations safe: a later optimistic mutation's placeholder survives an earlier mutation's rollback, even on the same entry; a fetch result that arrived in the meantime is newer than the failed closure and is kept; a later mutation that wrote directly on top of the failed one inherits its restore point, so if it fails too the entry goes back to before both. Stamps are compared, never contents, so two writes of equal data are still distinguishable. This behaviour is covered by the optimistic-rollback contract scenario on all three platforms.

A mutation marked idempotent that fails with a network error while the Connectivity port says the device is offline is not lost. It is appended to a persisted queue (the Kv key keel.query.queue) with its parameters and an idempotency key, and replayed in order when connectivity returns. The request carries an Idempotency-Key header that stays the same across retries and replays, so a server can tell a repeat from a second item. rust #[keel::mutation(key = "remote-todos:{list}", idempotent)] pub async fn post_remote_todo(ctx: &Ctx, list: String, title: String) -> Result<RemoteTodo, RemoteError> { // … if let Some(key) = keel::query::idempotency_key() { request = request.with_header("Idempotency-Key", key.to_string()); } // … } A mutation that is not idempotent fails immediately when offline. While a queued call waits, the optimistic placeholder stays visible, and the caller's await keeps waiting until the network returns and the request is replayed.

Entries marked persist are written to the Kv port after each successful fetch (debounced, 250 ms) and read back when the core starts. Each entry stores the schema hash it was written under, and an entry from a different schema is dropped rather than decoded wrongly.

Because the network is a port, a query is tested with a scripted fake and no sockets. FakeHttp answers from rules and records every request, including a flaky endpoint: rust let http = FakeHttp::new(); // two timeouts, then success for ever after http.respond_sequence("https://x.test/a", [Err(HttpError::Timeout), Err(HttpError::Timeout)]); http.respond("https://x.test/a", HttpResponse::new(200, b"ok".to_vec())); Pair it with FakeClock to advance time and ScriptedConnectivity to go offline. The core never touches the outside world directly. Time, randomness, the network, storage and the app's lifecycle all come through ports: traits the platform implements and the core calls.

A port is a Rust trait marked #[keel::port]. The platform implements it (an adapter), or a Rust fake does in a test. The core calls it through the context, for example ctx.http().request(req).await, and does not know or care what is behind it. That is what keeps the core deterministic (rule R12): it has no wall clock, no random source and no threads outside the Clock, Rng and Timer ports and the runtime. There are three kinds, and the kind decides how a call travels: Kind Meaning sync the platform answers before the call returns. A port is sync only if every method is sync async the platform answers later; the core's task waits, and can be cancelled event fire and forget from the platform into the core, such as "connectivity changed"

Port Kind Methods Clock sync now_ms() -> i64, monotonic_ns() -> u64 Rng sync fill(len) -> Bytes Log sync log(level, target, message) Http async request(HttpRequest) -> Result<HttpResponse, HttpError> Kv async get, set, delete, list(prefix) SecureStore async the same shape as Kv, for secrets Fs async read, write, delete, list, each returning Result<_, FsError> Timer sync set(timer_id, delay_ms); the platform answers later with a timer-fired event Connectivity event changed(online, kind) with NetKind of Wifi, Cellular, Wired, Unknown or None Lifecycle event changed(state) with AppState of Active, Inactive or Background They exchange a small set of types: HttpRequest (method, url, headers, optional body, optional timeout), HttpResponse (status, headers, body), HttpError (Network, Timeout, Cancelled, InvalidUrl), Header, FsError (NotFound, Denied, Io), NetKind and AppState. These ports and types ship inside each platform runtime and are not generated into your app's bindings. Every core links keel-ports, so its schema contains them and the schema hash covers them, but the generator leaves them out and the generated code refers to the runtime's own types. You replace a default when you load the core. The playground replaces Http with an in-memory server (so it needs no backend) and Kv with a map: web/src/keel.ts const adapters = { http: server, kv: memoryKv() }; await KeelCore.load({ mode: "wasm-main", wasm: new URL(wasmUrl, location.href), expectedSchemaHash: KeelIds.schemaHash, adapters, }); ios/PlaygroundApp/KeelBootstrap.swift let adapters = Adapters.platformDefault .removing(portId: fnv1a32("port.Connectivity")) .replacing(PlaygroundNetwork.shared) .replacing(KvAdapter(directory: store)) try KeelCore.load(.inproc(adapters: adapters, expectedSchemaHash: KeelIds.schemaHash)) android/.../KeelApp.kt KeelCore.load( LoadOptions( expectedSchemaHash = KeelIds.SCHEMA_HASH, adapters = mapOf( StandardPorts.Http.PORT_ID to server.portImpl(), StandardPorts.Kv.PORT_ID to InMemoryKv().portImpl(), ), ), ) Register the ports your core needs at load time. A core's start-up work (query hydration reads the Kv port) runs as soon as the runtime exists, so a port registered later can be missed by that work.

An unavailable port is a normal outcome, not a bug. A port nobody registered behaves as unavailable, a call can be cancelled, and a host can reply with bytes that do not decode. The core handles all three without panicking: If the port method returns Result<T, E>, the failure becomes an E. HttpError and FsError implement From<PortError>, so an unavailable Http port is Network("the Http port has no adapter registered"). Your own error type needs the same conversion, and the macro checks it at compile time (E0033). If the method has no error channel, there is no typed way to say "unavailable", so the call panics with a message that names the port and method and says how to bind one (E0062). The runtime contains that panic at the boundary. Give optional ports a Result, or register them.

Mark a trait with #[keel::port]. The macro registers it in the schema and generates a proxy type, so the core calls your trait like any other, and the platform gets a protocol or interface to implement. This one is made up, to show the shape: rust #[keel::port(sync)] pub trait Haptics { fn tap(&self, strength: u8); } A port method's parameters must be wire types (E0030), and an event port's methods cannot return a value (E0031).

Every standard port has a deterministic Rust fake in keel::ports::fakes. They are all Send + Sync, keep state behind a lock, and never read the system clock, a random source or a thread. One binary runs the whole loop: scaffold a project, generate bindings, build the core for each platform, serve it live, and check your machine. Every command teaches through its own help.

One schema feeds three generators. Three runtimes hold the mirrors. A small binary wire carries writes in and change-sets out. This page is the tour, and the specification in the repository is the contract.

Keel is a Rust core, a schema extracted from it, three code generators, and three platform runtimes. Your screens sit on generated bindings; the bindings sit on a runtime package; the runtime talks to the core through a transport that is an ABI, not a framework. Each platform has the same four layers; only the bottom one is platform-specific machinery. The core is one codebase. On each platform it is linked the way that platform expects: a static library in an XCFramework on iOS, libkeel_core.so over JNI on Android, a wasm module on the web. During development the same core can instead run on your machine behind a WebSocket (keel dev).

Everything is derived from the schema. Bindgen emits three trees that depend only on the matching runtime package. Everything starts with the macros. #[keel::api], #[keel::store], #[keel::port] and friends validate your code and register a description of each public type and function. Collected together, those descriptions are the schema: records, enums, objects, stores with their signals, functions, ports and queries. The CLI builds your core as a host library, loads it, asks for the schema, and hands it to keel bindgen, which writes a Swift package, a Gradle module and an npm package. Generated code depends only on the matching runtime package. Three properties of this design are worth stating plainly: Names become ids at compile time. A type id is a hash of its name, a method id a hash of Type.method, a port id a hash of port.Trait, and a signal id is its position among the store's signal fields. Every platform agrees without a registry lookup. The hash is FNV-1a. The schema has a hash. It is the FNV-1a hash of a canonical form: lists sorted by name, no whitespace, doc comments excluded, so two cores with the same public surface hash the same. Each binding carries the hash it …

The wire is small on purpose. It is little-endian throughout, with no alignment and no padding. All lengths are u32. Decoders never panic on malformed input; they return a typed error. In-process calls skip it and carry only the payload. The envelope frames every message on the WebSocket and worker transports. In-process calls carry only the payload. The native boundary is a C ABI, exported with #[unsafe(no_mangle)] extern "C" and nothing but C-compatible types. The whole surface is nineteen functions (parameter lists abridged here): c uint32_t keel_abi_version(void); uint64_t keel_schema_hash(void); KeelBuf keel_schema_json(void); uint32_t keel_init(cfg, len, reply_cb, changeset_cb, stream_cb, user); void keel_shutdown(void); uint32_t keel_call(ptr, len); // async reply arrives on reply_cb KeelBuf keel_call_sync(ptr, len); // reply returned directly void keel_cancel(call_id); void keel_stream_credit(call_id, credit); void keel_observe(handle, signal_id, on); void keel_release(handle); void keel_port_register(port_id, cb, user); void keel_port_reply(ptr, len); void keel_event(port_id, method_id, ptr, len); void keel_timer_fired(timer_id); KeelBuf keel_snapshot(void); uint32_t keel_restore(ptr, len); KeelBuf keel_stats_json(void); void keel_buf_free(KeelBuf buf); Android reaches the same functions through a JNI shim that registers its natives once at load, so there is no per-call lookup. The web has no wasm-bindgen: the module exports and imports use only i32, i64 and f64, a 64-bit handle is passed as two halves, and …

One mutator. The core has one lock. Whoever holds it is the core loop. A synchronous call from the host runs on the caller's thread holding that lock, so it costs a mutex acquire, not a thread hop. Async work. Async calls are tasks on a small executor with no tokio, polled by the core thread, one task per in-flight call. Cancelling a call drops its future. A blocking pool runs blocking work off the lock. It must not write signals, and debug builds refuse such writes. wasm is single threaded. The host calls keel_poll() on the next microtask whenever the core asks to be scheduled. Shutdown is orderly. Every call still in flight is answered as cancelled and every stream ends, each exactly once, before the threads are joined.

Mode Where the core runs Used for in-process linked into the app (C ABI on iOS, JNI on Android) shipping wasm-main a wasm module on the page's main thread simple web apps wasm-worker the same module in a worker web apps that want the main thread free remote your machine, behind a WebSocket keel dev Platform runtimes do the same jobs everywhere: load the core, allocate call ids, map replies to continuations, hold the mirror and apply change-sets on the main thread, implement observe and release, provide default adapters, implement the codecs, and refuse a mismatched core with a clear error that names both hashes.

A UI and a core that were not built from the same schema must not talk. The schema hash is checked when the runtime attaches and surfaces as a typed mismatch error, and keel bindgen --check catches stale bindings at build time. Breaking the wire is a major version and needs an ADR; evolving a schema across a hash mismatch is deliberately not in v1.

Generated Swift is written the way a Swift engineer would write it by hand: value types, typed throws, async/await, AsyncSequence and an @Observable store. Swift 6 language mode, strict concurrency, no Objective-C. keel bindgen writes a Swift package (Sources/<Module>/Generated/*.swift and a Package.swift) that depends only on KeelRuntime. The shapes below come from the playground's generated code and the specification (§10.1).

Attach the app to its core once, before any store is created. The runtime checks the core's schema hash against the one the bindings were generated from and throws a clear error if they differ. KeelBootstrap.swift import KeelRuntime import PlaygroundCore @MainActor static func start() throws { let adapters = Adapters.platformDefault // URLSession, Keychain, files, … .replacing(PlaygroundNetwork.shared) // swap one port try KeelCore.load(.inproc(adapters: adapters, expectedSchemaHash: KeelIds.schemaHash)) } In debug builds you can attach to the core that keel dev serves instead, with KeelCore.load(.remote(url: url, adapters: adapters, expectedSchemaHash: KeelIds.schemaHash)). After loading, every generated type defaults to the shared core: try Todos() is try Todos(ctx: .shared).

Rust Swift bool, f32, f64 Bool, Float, Double i8 … i64, u8 … u64 Int8 … Int64, UInt8 … UInt64 String, Bytes String, [UInt8] Duration, Timestamp, Uuid Duration, Date, UUID Option<T>, Vec<T> T?, [T] Map<K, V> [K: V] record, enum, error struct, enum, enum conforming to Error Names follow the platform: Rust snake_case becomes camelCase for methods and fields and PascalCase for types, and enum variants become lowerCamel cases.

A record is a struct: Sendable, Hashable and Codable, with a memberwise initializer. swift /// One item of the to-do list. public struct Todo: KeelRecord, Sendable, Hashable, Codable { public var id: UUID public var title: String public var done: Bool public init(id: UUID, title: String, done: Bool) } The wire codec (keelEncode, keelDecode) is generated beside it and is not something you call.

A unit enum is a UInt16-backed enum that is also CaseIterable, so it works directly in a Picker. A data enum carries its fields as associated values. swift public enum Filter: UInt16, KeelEnum, CaseIterable, Sendable, Codable { case all = 0, active = 1, done = 2 } public enum Figure: KeelEnum, Sendable, Hashable { case circle(radius: Double) case rect(width: Double, height: Double) case label(String) case empty }

A Rust #[keel::error] becomes a Swift enum conforming to Error (and LocalizedError, with the message from #[error("…")]). Functions that can fail use typed throws. swift public enum TodoError: KeelError, Error, Sendable, Hashable { case emptyTitle // "the title cannot be empty" // a variant that wraps another error carries it: case http(HttpError) } do { let todo = try await todos.add(title: draft) } catch { // `error` is a TodoError, not a string to parse print(error.localizedDescription) } Typed throws needs Swift 6. keel.toml has swift_typed_throws = false for code that must still emit plain throws. A failure the shape of the API cannot express (a core panic, a malformed reply, schema drift) stops the process with a message, because it means the core and the bindings disagree.

An object is a final class holding a handle into the core. Sync methods are plain functions, async methods are async, and stream methods return an AsyncThrowingStream. A free Rust function is a free Swift function that takes the core last. swift public final class Probe: KeelObject, @unchecked Sendable { public init(ctx: KeelCore = .shared) throws // the constructor `new` public func counters() -> ProbeCounters // sync public func wait(ms: UInt32) async throws -> UInt32 // async public func ticks(count: UInt32) -> AsyncThrowingStream<UInt32, Error> // stream } public func add(a: Int32, b: Int32, ctx: KeelCore = .shared) -> Int32 public func area(_ figure: Figure, ctx: KeelCore = .shared) throws(LabError) -> Double Sync methods on an in-process core call straight into the core (keel_call_sync). Streams apply real backpressure: the generated code grants credit as your loop consumes items, and dropping the stream stops it in the core. Release an object with close(), which is idempotent. deinit is only a backstop for objects that go out of scope without it, so hold an object for as long as you need its state.

A store is an @Observable class on the MainActor. Every signal is a public private(set) var, so SwiftUI tracks reads and re-renders when a change-set is applied. Computed signals are read-only properties the core keeps up to date. swift @MainActor @Observable public final class Todos: KeelStore { public private(set) var todos: [Todo] public private(set) var filter: Filter public private(set) var visible: [Todo] // computed by the core public private(set) var remaining: UInt32 // computed by the core public init(ctx: KeelCore = .shared) throws public func setFilter(_ f: Filter) public func add(title: String) async throws(TodoError) -> Todo } Reading todos.visible is a plain property read: it never calls into the core. The initial values are decoded from the change-set the core emits when the store starts observing during init. swift struct TodosScreen: View { let todos: Todos var body: some View { List(todos.visible, id: \.id) { todo in Button(todo.title) { todos.toggle(id: todo.id) } } .toolbar { ToolbarItem(placement: .principal) { Text("\(todos.remaining) left") } } } }

A #[keel::query] becomes a store with five signals: data, status, error, fetching and updatedAt, plus refetch() and invalidate(). Construct one to observe the query; it fetches when the data is missing or stale. swift let inbox = try RemoteTodosQueryHandle(list: "inbox") // inbox.data: [RemoteTodo]?, inbox.status, inbox.fetching, inbox.error, inbox.updatedAt See Queries & mutations for what the core does behind it.

The ten standard ports are implemented by KeelRuntime (URLSession, Keychain, FileManager, NWPathMonitor and so on) and are not generated into your module. A port you define yourself becomes a protocol your app implements and registers with the adapters: swift public protocol Http: KeelPort { func request(_ req: HttpRequest) async throws(HttpError) -> HttpResponse } See Ports & adapters for the defaults and for swapping one.

Change-sets are applied on the MainActor, in one hop per transaction, so observable properties only ever change on the main thread. Stores and objects release their handle on close(), with deinit as the backstop. KeelCore.stats() exposes live handle counts for tests. Swift 6 strict concurrency is on. Generated stores are @MainActor; objects are @unchecked Sendable because the core serializes access behind its lock.

Generated Kotlin is what a Kotlin engineer would write by hand: data classes, sealed hierarchies, suspend functions, Flow, and StateFlows you read with collectAsState(). The runtime needs only the standard library and kotlinx-coroutines. keel bindgen writes a Gradle module (src/main/kotlin/<package>/*.kt, a build.gradle.kts and a .gitignore) that depends only on keel-runtime. The shapes below come from the playground's generated code and the specification (§10.2).

Attach the app to its core once per process, before any store is created, typically in Application.onCreate. KeelCore.load checks that the native library was built from the same schema as the bindings. KeelApp.kt class KeelApp : Application() { override fun onCreate() { super.onCreate() KeelCore.load( LoadOptions( expectedSchemaHash = KeelIds.SCHEMA_HASH, adapters = mapOf(StandardPorts.Http.PORT_ID to myHttp.portImpl()), ), ) } } The core is libkeel_core.so, which keel build --platform android writes to build/android/jniLibs/<abi>/. On Android the runtime installs the adapters that need nothing from the platform (Clock, Rng, Log, Timer); pass the others you want to replace. After loading, every generated type defaults to the shared core: Todos() is Todos(ctx = KeelCore.shared).

Rust Kotlin bool, f32, f64 Boolean, Float, Double i8 … i64 Byte, Short, Int, Long u8 … u64 UByte, UShort, UInt, ULong String, Bytes String, ByteArray Duration, Timestamp, Uuid Duration, Timestamp, UUID Option<T>, Vec<T> T?, List<T> Map<K, V> Map<K, V> record, enum, error data class, enum class or sealed interface, sealed class Names follow the platform: Rust snake_case becomes camelCase for functions and properties and PascalCase for types. Unit enum variants become UPPER_SNAKE constants; data enum variants become PascalCase classes. Keel does not support Option<Option<T>> because Kotlin cannot express nested optionality (E0063).
kotlin /** One item of the to-do list. */ data class Todo( val id: UUID, val title: String, val done: Boolean, ) : KeelRecord

A unit enum is an enum class with its wire index. A data enum is a sealed interface whose variants are data classes, data objects for the ones without fields. kotlin enum class Filter(val index: UShort) : KeelEnum { ALL(0u), ACTIVE(1u), DONE(2u); } sealed interface Figure : KeelEnum { data class Circle(val radius: Double) : Figure data class Rect(val width: Double, val height: Double) : Figure data class Label(val value: String) : Figure data object Empty : Figure } when (figure) over a sealed interface is exhaustive, so adding a variant in Rust is a compile error in every when that forgot it.

A #[keel::error] becomes a sealed class extending KeelException, with the message from #[error("…")]. A failing suspend function throws the typed error, so catch (e: TodoError) and when (e) work. kotlin sealed class TodoError(message: String) : KeelException(message) { data object EmptyTitle : TodoError("the title cannot be empty") // a variant wrapping another error carries it: data class Http(val cause: HttpError) } viewModelScope.launch { try { store.add(draft) } catch (e: TodoError) { problem = when (e) { TodoError.EmptyTitle -> "Give it a title first." } } }

An object is a class holding a handle into the core. Sync methods are plain functions, async methods are suspend, and stream methods return a Flow. A free Rust function is a top-level Kotlin function that takes the core as its last, defaulted parameter. kotlin class Probe private constructor(core: KeelCore, handle: Long) : KeelObject(core, handle) { fun counters(): ProbeCounters // sync suspend fun wait(ms: UInt): UInt // async, cancellable fun ticks(count: UInt): Flow<UInt> // stream companion object { fun create(ctx: KeelCore = KeelCore.shared): Probe } } fun add(a: Int, b: Int, ctx: KeelCore = KeelCore.shared): Int suspend fun createRemoteTodo(list: String, title: String, ctx: KeelCore = KeelCore.shared): RemoteTodo Cancelling the coroutine cancels the call in the core, and a Flow applies backpressure: the runtime grants credit as your collector consumes items. The runtime contains core panics at the boundary, so a bug in the core is a typed failure, not a crash.

A store extends KeelStore. Every signal is a read-only StateFlow; computed signals are updated by the core. Read them in Compose with collectAsState(), no extra module needed. kotlin class Todos : KeelStore { val todos: StateFlow<List<Todo>> val filter: StateFlow<Filter> val visible: StateFlow<List<Todo>> // computed by the core val remaining: StateFlow<UInt> // computed by the core constructor(ctx: KeelCore = KeelCore.shared) fun setFilter(f: Filter) suspend fun add(title: String): Todo // throws TodoError } kotlin @Composable fun TodosScreen(vm: TodosViewModel = viewModel()) { val visible by vm.store.visible.collectAsState() val remaining by vm.store.remaining.collectAsState() Text("$remaining left") LazyColumn { // the list is keyed by id in the core, so Compose moves and animates rows items(visible, key = { it.id }) { todo -> TodoRow(todo) } } } Hold on to the store. The runtime's mirror holds a store weakly. A StateFlow on its own does not keep the store, and the core object behind it, alive. Keep the store in a ViewModel and close it in onCleared().

A #[keel::query] becomes a store with five StateFlows (data, status, error, fetching, updatedAt) plus refetch() and invalidate(). Constructing it observes the query and fetches when the data is missing or stale. kotlin val inbox = RemoteTodosQueryHandle.create("inbox") val items by inbox.data.collectAsState() // List<RemoteTodo>? val busy by inbox.fetching.collectAsState() See Queries & mutations.

The ten standard ports are implemented in dev.keel.runtime.adapters (OkHttp or HttpURLConnection, SharedPreferences-backed files, EncryptedFile, ConnectivityManager, ProcessLifecycleOwner and so on) and are not generated into your module. You replace one by passing an implementation in LoadOptions.adapters, keyed by its port id. A port you define yourself becomes an interface: kotlin interface Http : KeelPort { suspend fun request(req: HttpRequest): HttpResponse // throws HttpError } See Ports & adapters for the defaults. Android-specific adapters live in the android-adapters module, not in the runtime.

Signals are updated on Dispatchers.Main.immediate, in one hop per transaction. On a JVM without Android the runtime falls back to a single-thread executor, which is what the JVM test suite uses. KeelStore and KeelObject implement AutoCloseable. Call close() to release the handle (a use { } block works); a Cleaner releases leaked handles as a backstop. KeelCore.stats() exposes live handle counts. Over JNI, callbacks arrive from core threads and are decoded immediately; you never see a raw buffer.

Generated TypeScript is strict-mode ESM with no any in exported types: plain interfaces and unions for data, promises for calls, signals for state, and hooks for React. The core package has no runtime dependencies. keel bindgen writes an npm package (src/*.ts, package.json, tsconfig.json) that imports only from @keel/runtime. The shapes below come from the playground's generated code and the specification (§10.3).

Load the core once, before you create a store. The runtime compares the core's schema hash with the one the bindings were generated from and rejects a mismatch with KeelSchemaMismatch. web/src/keel.ts import { KeelCore } from "@keel/runtime"; import { KeelIds, Todos } from "@playground/core"; import wasmUrl from "../../build/web/keel_core.wasm?url"; await KeelCore.load({ mode: "wasm-main", // the core runs in a wasm module on this thread wasm: new URL(wasmUrl, location.href), expectedSchemaHash: KeelIds.schemaHash, adapters: { http, kv }, // optional: replace a default adapter }); const todos = await Todos.create(); // uses KeelCore.shared mode Where the core runs "wasm-main" a wasm module on the page's main thread "wasm-worker" the same module in a worker, keeping the main thread free "remote" the core that keel dev serves, over a WebSocket: { mode: "remote", url: "ws://127.0.0.1:7443", expectedSchemaHash }

Rust TypeScript bool boolean i8 … i32, u8 … u32, f32, f64 number i64, u64 bigint (or number with #[keel(js_number)] / ts_js_number) String, Bytes string, Uint8Array Duration, Timestamp, Uuid Duration, Timestamp, string Option<T>, Vec<T> T | null, T[] Map<K, V> Map<K, V> record interface unit enum, data enum string-literal union, discriminated union on kind error a class extending KeelError, with subclasses per variant 64-bit integers become bigint so no value is ever silently rounded; a 64-bit value outside the safe range is a decode error rather than a wrong number when you opt into number.

ts /** One item of the to-do list. */ export interface Todo { id: string; title: string; done: boolean } export type Filter = "all" | "active" | "done"; export type Figure = | { kind: "circle"; radius: number } | { kind: "rect"; width: number; height: number } | { kind: "label"; value: string } | { kind: "empty" }; A switch (figure.kind) over the union is exhaustive under strict, so adding a variant in Rust breaks every switch that forgot it.

A #[keel::error] becomes an abstract class with a kind and one subclass per variant, so you can branch with instanceof or on kind. A rejected call carries the typed error, not a string to parse. ts export abstract class TodoError extends KeelError { readonly kind: "emptyTitle"; } export namespace TodoError { export class EmptyTitle extends TodoError { /* message: "the title cannot be empty" */ } } try { await todos.add(draft); } catch (error) { if (error instanceof TodoError) setProblem(error.message); }

An object is a class holding a handle. Every method returns a Promise, which keeps the API uniform across main-thread, worker and remote modes. Stream methods return an AsyncIterable, and any call takes an optional AbortSignal as its last argument to cancel it in the core. ts export class Probe extends KeelObject { static create(core?: KeelCore): Promise<Probe>; counters(): Promise<ProbeCounters>; wait(ms: number, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<number>; ticks(count: number): AsyncIterable<number>; // backpressure through stream credit } export function add(a: number, b: number): Promise<number>; Release an object with close() (idempotent) or with using where Symbol.dispose exists (Node 20+ and current browsers); a FinalizationRegistry is the backstop.

A store extends KeelStore. Every signal is a read-only Signal<T>: get() returns the current value, peek() reads without subscribing, and subscribe(fn) calls you on change and returns an unsubscribe function. Computed signals are written by the core. ts export class Todos extends KeelStore { readonly todos: Signal<Todo[]>; readonly filter: Signal<Filter>; readonly visible: Signal<Todo[]>; // computed by the core readonly remaining: Signal<number>; // computed by the core static create(core?: KeelCore): Promise<Todos>; setFilter(f: Filter): Promise<void>; add(title: string, signal?: AbortSignal): Promise<Todo>; } Change-sets are batched with queueMicrotask into one flush per macrotask, so several signals that changed in one transaction update together and a component never renders a half-applied state.

@keel/runtime/react exports two hooks. useSignal is useSyncExternalStore over a signal, with a server snapshot. useKeel creates a store when the component mounts and closes it when it unmounts; it returns undefined until the store exists, and useSignal accepts an undefined signal. tsx import { useKeel, useSignal } from "@keel/runtime/react"; export function CounterView() { const counter = useKeel(Counter); // undefined until created const count = useSignal(counter?.count); const parity = useSignal(counter?.parity); // computed in the core, same change-set if (counter === undefined) return null; return <button onClick={() => void counter.increment()}>{count} ({parity})</button>; } Adapters ship for the other frameworks as thin files, exported from @keel/runtime/vue (useSignal as a shallowRef, useKeel), /svelte (signalStore, a Readable) and /solid (useSignal as an Accessor, useKeel). The frameworks are optional peer dependencies; the core package imports none of them.

A #[keel::query] becomes a store with five signals (data, status, error, fetching, updatedAt) plus refetch() and invalidate(). ts const inbox = await RemoteTodosQueryHandle.create("inbox"); const items = useSignal(inbox.data); // RemoteTodo[] | null const busy = useSignal(inbox.fetching); await inbox.refetch(); See Queries & mutations.

The ten standard ports and their types are exported from @keel/runtime and are not generated into your package. The browser defaults use fetch, IndexedDB, OPFS, setTimeout, navigator.onLine and visibilitychange; Node uses fetch and files. Replace one with adapters in KeelCore.load. A port you define yourself becomes an interface: ts export interface Http extends KeelPort { request(req: HttpRequest): Promise<HttpResponse>; } See Ports & adapters.

The runtime is testable without a browser: over the remote transport against a native core, and against a WAT stub of the wasm ABI. The contract suite runs the same scenarios as the Swift and Kotlin runners, against the real wasm module.
